new_statements.quote: Sema Lima p. 150: "We can conclude from our data above that Mungaka can be classified as both a register and tone language, as it employs both level and falling/rising tones. It is also obvious that Mungaka, being a tone language, differs considerably from both English and French, which are stress-timed and syllable-timed, respectively. However, Mungaka-speakers who are bilingual in French and English will agree that Mungaka is perhaps more akin to the former than the latter ... on close similarities in rhythm, both of which are perceived as isosyllabic, unlike English, which is isochronous (i.e., stressed-timed)." | Vielhauer 1915 p. 3: "Die Vokale werden bald lang (ā), bald kurz (a), bald mit Hochton (á), bald mit Mittel- (a), bald mit Tiefton (à) gesprochen. Es gibt auch noch Zwischentöne, die man aber in der Schrift nicht zu berücksichtigen braucht."
new_statements.translation: Vielhauer p. 3: 'The vowels are spoken now long (ā), now short (a), now with high tone (á), now with mid tone (a), now with low tone (à). There are also intermediate tones, which however need not be represented in writing.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Both first-hand descriptions treat Mungaka as a tone language (high/mid/low plus contour tones; tone also grammatical, e.g. future marked by raising the verb tone, Vielhauer p. 102) and give no rule for the location of word stress; Sema Lima only adds that Mungaka rhythm is syllable-based ('isosyllabic'), i.e. not stress-timed. No accessible source states where word stress falls in Mungaka specifically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Vielhauer's 'Betonung/betont' pp. 36-42 concern emphatic pronoun/genitive constructions, not word stress.)
new_statements.domain_note: The only positional stress claim found is genus-level, not Mungaka-specific: Anderson 2001 (in Mutaka & Chumbow eds., Research Mate in African Linguistics, p. 47; saved file), for Eastern Grassfields languages generally (Mungaka explicitly listed under Mbam-Nkam, p. 33; data from Ngiemboon): 'For nouns and verbs with single roots, it appears that the first syllable of the root is stressed. This means that all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed.' If the catalog admits genus-level inference this would read morphological-root (root-initial), but it is not a statement about Mungaka data. A Mungaka-specific stress discussion very probably exists in Nti 1986 (Yaoundé thesis; 15 in-volume hits for 'stress', 7 for 'stressed syllable'), which could supersede this reading.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted material concerns Mungaka of Bali-Nyonga (mung1266 proper; Vielhauer's 'Balisprache' = Mungaka of Ba'ni Nyonga, explicitly distinguished from the older Mubako' [Chamba] language). Glottolog's two 'phonology' refs (Nusi 2000 Ti; Ngueffo 1979 Bapi) describe the Bati (Ti) and Bapi/Bapakum varieties, not Bali-Nyonga speech. Anderson 2001's stress remark is a genus-level generalization for Eastern Grassfields illustrated from Ngiemboon (ngie1241? no: Ngiemboon = ngie1242), not Mungaka data.

sources.note: Family-level (Eastern Grassfields; Mungaka listed under Mbam-Nkam p. 33; examples from Ngiemboon). §6 Stress, p. 47: 'Stress phenomena have gone largely unmentioned in most descriptions of Bantoid languages... amplitude phenomena in these languages are mostly predictable... 6.1 Nouns and Verbs: First syllable of root. For nouns and verbs with single roots, it appears that the first syllable of the root is stressed. This means that all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed.' Functors: unresearched, probably unstressed.

sources.note: Lautlehre pp. 2-11 (Vokale, Konsonanten, Silbenbildung, Wortbildung). p. 3: 'Die Vokale werden bald lang (ā), bald kurz (a), bald mit Hochton (á), bald mit Mittel- (a), bald mit Tiefton (à) gesprochen. Es gibt auch noch Zwischentöne... Länge- und Tonzeichen werden nur gelegentlich zur Unterscheidung ähnlich klingender Wörter gesetzt.' Tone also grammatical (p. 102: future 'durch Hebung des Tons auf dem nackten Verb'). No section or sentence on word stress/Betonung: in-volume index hits for 'Betonung'/'betont' (pp. 36-42) are syntactic emphasis of pronouns/genitives; 'Akzent' 0 hits.
